title: The Groaning Creation
subtitle: The earth is the Lord's, and we were set in a garden to tend it, not to strip it.
question: If the world belongs to God and was handed to us to keep, what does our use of it say about whether we believe that?
whyItMatters: We did not make the world, and we will not get another one. It was spoken into being before us, declared good before we existed, and then placed into our hands with a single instruction that we have spent most of human history ignoring. To tend it. To keep it. The question of how we treat the soil and the water and the air is not a side issue for sentimental people who like trees. It is a question about whether we believe the earth is ours to do with as we please or God's to answer for.
biblicalFoundation:
In the first chapters of Genesis, before any law is given, before any covenant is cut, a man is placed in a garden and told to work it and to keep it. The Hebrew is plain. Avad and shamar. To serve and to guard. The very words later used for the priests who tended the tabernacle. This is the cultural mandate, and it is not a license. It is a vocation. Dominion in Genesis 1 is rule on behalf of a King who already owns everything, not rule as if we were kings ourselves.

The law that follows takes the same seriously. The land itself is given a sabbath. Every seventh year the fields were to lie unworked, because the land was not a machine to be run without rest and the people were not its owners but its tenants. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the Psalmist sings, the world and they that dwell therein. Not ours. His. We are tenants who have too often behaved as if the lease had no landlord.

And creation knows it. Paul writes that the whole creation groans together in the pains of childbirth, subjected to futility, waiting for the revealing of the sons of God. The damage we do is not invisible to the world that absorbs it. The groan is real. But so is the hope, because the same Christ who made all things is reconciling all things to himself, things in heaven and things on earth, making peace by the blood of his cross.

This is why the Christian hope was never escape. The promise at the end is not an evacuation from a burning planet but a renewed heaven and a renewed earth, a city coming down, the dwelling of God with men. The body is raised, not discarded. The creation is healed, not abandoned. If that is where the story ends, then how we treat the world now is not throwaway work on a doomed stage. It is the rehearsal of a future we say we believe in.
keyTexts: Genesis 2:15. The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and to keep it.
Leviticus 25:4-5. In the seventh year there shall be a sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a sabbath to the Lord.
Psalm 24:1. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the world and they that dwell therein.
Romans 8:19-22. The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now.
Colossians 1:19-20. Through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven.
Revelation 21:1-3. Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, and the dwelling place of God is with man.

churchRecord.led: There has always been a line of saints who loved the world precisely because they loved its Maker. Francis of Assisi preached to the creatures and called the sun and the moon his brother and sister, not as a pantheist but as a man overwhelmed that all of it belonged to one Father. The Celtic monks who read two books, scripture and creation, and would not despise the second. The Benedictine houses that practiced stewardship of land for a thousand years before the word was fashionable. And in our own time a real and growing creation-care movement, evangelicals and Catholics together insisting that to confess God as Creator is to accept a duty to what he created.
churchRecord.failed: But the church also baptized the very exploitation it should have rebuked. It blessed the felling of forests and the fouling of rivers as the march of progress and called it dominion. Worse, it grew a theology of escape, a reading in which the earth is a sinking ship and the only sane move is to get the souls off before it goes down. If it is all going to burn, why tend it. That sentence, spoken from pulpits and assumed in pews, did more to license neglect than any secular greed ever could. We taught people that the world did not matter, and they believed us, and they acted like it.

whereWeAgree: The earth is the Lord's. We did not make it and we do not own it. We were given it to keep, and we will answer for how we kept it. On this a faithful reading of scripture does not bend. Whatever else Christians dispute, the dispute is never over whether we are stewards. We are. The only question is what stewardship requires of us now.
captureLeft: The left capture takes a true love of the world and bends it into worship of the world. The creation, which was made to point past itself to its Maker, is treated as the highest thing, and the Creator quietly disappears. In its harder strands it becomes earth-worship and a recovered paganism, the planet personified as a goddess to be appeased. It develops an anti-human reflex, learning to speak of people as a plague, a virus, a cancer on the body of the earth, as if the one creature made in God's image were the one creature the earth would be better without. And it turns the climate crisis into an apocalypse with no redemption in it, a doom that fills the whole sky, so that the crisis itself stands where the Creator used to stand and despair does the work that repentance was meant to do.
captureRight: The right capture takes the word dominion and reads it as a license to use up. It hears subdue the earth and hears nothing about serve and keep. In its convenient form it denies that we bear any real responsibility at all, treating every warning as alarmism and every call to restraint as a threat. It leans on the worst of the escapist theology, the it-is-all-going-to-burn shrug that turns the end of the world into an excuse for the abuse of the world. And it has learned to treat stewardship itself as a partisan plot, so that the moment a believer says we ought to care for what God made, he is sorted into the enemy camp and dismissed before he has finished the sentence. We have let our politics tell us what our Bibles are allowed to say.
whereWeDiffer: Here the honest line has to be drawn. The call to stewardship is not contested among faithful Christians. The science and the economics and the policy of climate are. Faithful believers who agree completely that the earth is the Lord's can still read the data differently, weigh the trade-offs differently, and land in genuinely different places on carbon, on energy, on regulation, on cost, and on who bears it. These are prudential judgments, the kind scripture does not settle for us, the kind that require humility from everyone holding one. To make a particular policy the test of faith is to claim a certainty the question does not give us. The duty to care is commanded. The means of caring is argued. We must not confuse the two, and we keep confusing the two.
theCost: To take this seriously costs something, and the cost is why we avoid it. It costs the right its alliance with an economics that would rather not be asked questions. It costs the left its tidy story in which humanity is the villain and the planet the saint. It costs all of us the comfort of the escape hatch, the quiet relief of believing none of this finally matters because we are leaving anyway. And it costs me personally, because I drive what I drive and buy what I buy and have rarely let the doctrine of creation touch a single decision I made on a Tuesday. The indictment is not out there. It is in my own garage.
charge: Go back to the garden and read the instruction again. Work it and keep it. Then look at the small piece of the world that is actually in your hands, the yard, the street, the habits, the appetite, the vote, the waste, and ask what keeping it would look like if you believed it belonged to God. Not the planet in the abstract. The patch of it you touch. Tend that, as a tenant who knows the landlord is coming home.

right.label: Dominion as license
right.whatItLooksLike: Stewardship is read out of the text entirely. Subdue the earth is heard as use it up, the word keep is forgotten, and any call to restraint is treated as an attack from the other team. Responsibility is denied, escape is assumed, and care for creation is filed under partisan suspicion.
right.inThePast: The doctrine of dominion was pressed into service to bless the clearing of forests, the draining of wetlands, and the fouling of rivers as simple progress. Alongside it grew a popular end-times reading in which the world was a doomed stage, so that its ruin could be met with a shrug rather than a grief.
right.now: The reflex hardened into political identity. To question consumption or pollution became coded as belonging to the other side, and so a plain biblical duty was abandoned not on theological grounds but tribal ones. The escape-hatch theology still does quiet service, excusing neglect with the assurance that it is all going to burn.
named: The escapist end-times reading that treats a burning world as reason for indifference rather than grief
The alignment of creation-denial with partisan identity, so that care for the earth is dismissed as belonging to the enemy
The Cornwall Alliance and its declaration framing environmental concern as a threat to the poor and to the gospel
The misreading of subdue and dominion as ownership rather than stewardship under a King
The reduction of restraint to alarmism, refusing any human responsibility for measurable harm
The prosperity-adjacent assumption that the earth is an inexhaustible supply to be drawn down without account

left.label: Creation worshipped
left.whatItLooksLike: The world is loved past its proper place until it takes the place of its Maker. The creature is adored and the Creator forgotten. Humanity is reframed as the enemy of the planet, and the crisis swells until it fills the whole sky, leaving despair where repentance and hope were meant to be.
left.inThePast: Romantic and pantheist strands long treated nature as the divine itself, the planet as a living goddess, the wild as more holy than the human. The instinct to revere the world slid into the instinct to worship it, and the line between honoring what God made and deifying it was quietly erased.
left.now: The same instinct returns as a climate apocalypticism with no redemption in it, and as an anti-human framing in which people are described as a plague upon the earth. Anti-natalist arguments follow, treating the having of children as harm, and the crisis itself comes to occupy the place once held by the Creator.
named: Deep ecology and its valuation of the non-human world above the human
Earth-worship and neo-pagan strands that personify the planet as a deity to be appeased
Anti-natalism that frames the bearing of children as a wrong done to the earth
Climate apocalypticism that preaches doom without redemption and despair without repentance
The anti-human framing that speaks of people as a virus, a plague, or a cancer on the planet
The Gaia personification that grants the earth a will and a sanctity owed only to its Maker
The displacement of the Creator by the crisis, so that the emergency itself becomes the object of ultimate fear
